passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — peremptory norms of general international law from which no derogation is permitted — occupies a peculiar and contested position within the architecture of the international legal order. Unlike ordinary treaty obligations, which bind only consenting states and may be modified by subsequent agreement among the parties, jus cogens norms are held to supersede inconsistent treaty provisions and, in the view of many theorists, to invalidate customary international law that conflicts with them. The 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties codified this hierarchy, providing in its Articles 53 and 64 that any treaty conflicting with a peremptory norm is void ab initio, or, in the case of a subsequently emerging norm, void from the moment of that norm's crystallization. Yet the Convention offers no catalogue of which norms qualify as peremptory, and the International Law Commission's efforts over subsequent decades to enumerate them have yielded only a short and contested list — the prohibitions on genocide, slavery, torture, and aggression among states being the least controversial entries.

The conceptual difficulty runs deeper than the absence of an authoritative catalogue. For a norm to achieve peremptory status under the Convention's own criteria, it must be "accepted and recognized by the international community of states as a whole" — a formulation that imports a kind of tacit consent that sits uneasily with the claim that jus cogens norms bind states regardless of their assent. Scholars advancing a natural-law reading argue that the norms' peremptory character derives from their moral content, not from any act of state recognition; on this view, recognition is merely declaratory rather than constitutive. Legal positivists, by contrast, insist that a rule cannot simultaneously depend on state consent for its validity and purport to override that same consent when inconvenient. This tension has never been satisfactorily resolved, and it generates concrete doctrinal instability: domestic courts confronting claims of immunity for heads of state accused of torture must decide whether the jus cogens prohibition on torture has displaced the customary rule of sovereign immunity without any reliable mechanism for determining whether both norms operate at the same hierarchical tier.

Furthermore, the principle of lex specialis — the rule that a more specific legal norm prevails over a more general one in cases of conflict — complicates any straightforward application of jus cogens supremacy. In a series of provisional measures orders issued between 1999 and 2007, an international tribunal declined to treat jus cogens arguments as automatically displacing lex specialis regimes established by regional treaty frameworks, reasoning that the parties had crafted a self-contained regime intended to govern disputes exhaustively within its own terms. Critics of these orders argued that permitting lex specialis to trump jus cogens in procedural contexts effectively circumvents the hierarchy the Vienna Convention was designed to entrench. The tribunal's position was, in this respect, regrettably formalistic: where a peremptory norm is at stake, one ought not to permit the procedural architecture of a specialized regime to insulate state conduct from scrutiny under the broadest obligations the international community has chosen to recognize.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's codification of jus cogens norms has rendered the international legal order more hierarchical than it was before 1969.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens, though codified in international treaty law, remains conceptually unstable and practically difficult to apply because of unresolved tensions involving consent, hierarchy, and competing legal principles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal positivists have identified a fatal internal contradiction in the Vienna Convention's account of jus cogens that renders the entire doctrine invalid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: International tribunals have consistently refused to apply jus cogens norms whenever lex specialis regimes are operative, thereby undermining the Vienna Convention.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The absence of an authoritative catalogue of peremptory norms is the primary obstacle to effective enforcement of jus cogens in domestic courts.

explanations.correct: The passage identifies three converging difficulties — the lack of a catalogue, the consent paradox debated by naturalists and positivists, and the lex specialis complication — and culminates in an editorial critique of the tribunal's formalism. B integrates all three strands into a thesis about conceptual instability and practical difficulty.
explanations.A: Too narrow and overstated: the passage does not claim the Convention succeeded in creating a cleaner hierarchy; indeed, it documents the hierarchy's fragility.
explanations.C: Overstates the positivist position: the passage says positivists have identified a tension they regard as unresolved, not that they have declared the doctrine invalid.
explanations.D: Misrepresents scope: the passage describes a specific series of tribunal orders, not a consistent pattern of refusal across all tribunals.
explanations.E: Too narrow: the absence of a catalogue is identified in paragraph one as one problem among several; the passage's larger concern is the deeper conceptual contradiction and the lex specialis conflict.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the international tribunal's provisional measures orders discussed in the third paragraph can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Measured approval, on the ground that regional treaty frameworks deserve deference when their drafters intended them to be self-contained.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Principled neutrality, since the author presents the tribunal's reasoning and its critics' objections without endorsing either.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Qualified disapproval, tempered by acknowledgment that the tribunal's position has some procedural merit in ordinary non-peremptory contexts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Outright condemnation, on the ground that the tribunal acted in deliberate bad faith toward the international community's established legal hierarchy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Critical disapproval expressed through editorial language, on the ground that procedural formalism should not insulate state conduct from scrutiny under peremptory norms.

explanations.correct: The author uses the editorial adverb 'regrettably' and issues a normative prescription ('one ought not to permit') in the final sentence of paragraph three, signaling clear disapproval grounded in the argument that procedural architecture should not trump peremptory norms.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's position: the author sides with the critics, not the tribunal.
explanations.B: Incorrect: the closing sentence is openly prescriptive — 'one ought not to permit' — so the author does take a side.
explanations.C: Partially plausible but wrong: the passage offers no qualification that the tribunal's approach might be acceptable in other contexts; the disapproval is unqualified within its stated scope.
explanations.D: Overstates intensity: 'regrettably formalistic' implies error, not bad faith; 'condemnation' and 'deliberate bad faith' exceed the author's register.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its codification described; the absence of a definitive enumeration of the doctrine's content is identified as its central weakness; and a solution proposed by international tribunals is evaluated and endorsed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its codified form described; an underlying conceptual tension in the doctrine is identified and two competing theoretical accounts of it are presented; and a further complication arising from a competing legal principle is described and critically assessed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A dispute between natural-law theorists and legal positivists is introduced; the historical origins of the dispute are traced through treaty law; and a series of tribunal rulings is cited as having resolved the dispute in favor of the positivist position.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's provisions are summarized; the author argues that these provisions are fundamentally incoherent; and an alternative framework grounded in natural law is proposed and defended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; its practical application in domestic courts is illustrated with a series of cases; and the passage concludes by calling for legislative reform to address identified inconsistencies.

explanations.correct: Paragraph one introduces jus cogens, describes its codification in the Vienna Convention, and notes the absence of an authoritative catalogue. Paragraph two identifies the deeper conceptual tension between consent-based validity and peremptory override, presenting the natural-law and positivist accounts. Paragraph three introduces the lex specialis complication via the tribunal orders and closes with the author's critical assessment. B tracks these three moves accurately.
explanations.A: Incorrect at the third step: the tribunal's position is criticized, not endorsed.
explanations.C: Misrepresents the passage's opening: paragraph one does not begin with the naturalist-positivist dispute; that appears in paragraph two. The tribunal orders do not resolve that dispute.
explanations.D: The author does not propose an alternative natural-law framework; the natural-law reading is mentioned as one theoretical account among two.
explanations.E: The passage includes one domestic-court example (sovereign immunity), but this is not 'a series of cases'; the passage does not call for legislative reform.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Articles 53 and 64 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties provide that a treaty conflicting with a jus cogens norm that arose after the treaty's conclusion is:

choices.label: A
choices.text: void ab initio, as though it had never been entered into.

choices.label: B
choices.text: void only if the parties to the treaty have expressly consented to subordination of their obligations to any subsequently emerging peremptory norm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: void from the moment the peremptory norm in question crystallized, rather than from the treaty's original conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: suspended but not voided, pending a determination by the International Law Commission as to whether the norm qualifies as peremptory.

choices.label: E
choices.text: subject to modification by the treaty parties so as to bring it into conformity with the emerging peremptory norm.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that a treaty conflicting with a subsequently emerging jus cogens norm is 'void from the moment of that norm's crystallization,' distinguishing this from the void ab initio rule that applies to treaties conflicting with pre-existing peremptory norms.
explanations.A: This describes the rule for treaties that conflicted with a jus cogens norm already in existence at the time of conclusion — not for subsequently emerging norms. The altered-qualifier trap.
explanations.B: The passage never mentions a consent-based exception for subsequent norms; this is invented.
explanations.D: No such suspension mechanism is mentioned in the passage; this is a plausible-world-fact trap.
explanations.E: The passage describes the consequence as voidness, not modification; this alters the key legal effect.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a legal positivist would regard which one of the following as a fundamental defect in the Vienna Convention's formulation of jus cogens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Convention fails to enumerate a comprehensive list of peremptory norms, leaving states uncertain about the content of their obligations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Convention's requirement of state recognition simultaneously grounds the validity of jus cogens norms in consent and claims that those norms override consent, producing an internal contradiction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Convention inadequately addresses the relationship between jus cogens norms and lex specialis regimes established by regional treaties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Convention adopts a natural-law methodology that is incompatible with the positivist foundations on which modern treaty law rests.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Convention's provisions on jus cogens were drafted without the participation of a sufficient number of states to constitute acceptance by the international community as a whole.

explanations.correct: The passage states that positivists 'insist that a rule cannot simultaneously depend on state consent for its validity and purport to override that same consent when inconvenient.' B is a precise paraphrase of this objection, which the passage attributes specifically to the positivist camp.
explanations.A: The passage identifies the lack of an authoritative catalogue as a problem, but does not attribute this concern specifically to positivists — it is a more general institutional observation.
explanations.C: The lex specialis complication is introduced in paragraph three as a separate doctrinal problem, not as the positivist objection. The passage does not attribute this concern to positivists.
explanations.D: This inverts the positivist critique: positivists are not objecting that the Convention is too positivist; they are objecting that the Convention's consent requirement is inconsistent with its peremptory-override claim.
explanations.E: No such drafting-participation claim appears in the passage; this is an outside-scope trap.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to domestic courts confronting immunity claims by heads of state accused of torture (second paragraph) serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: introduce a separate legal problem concerning the scope of sovereign immunity that the remainder of the passage addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate that natural-law theorists are more successful than legal positivists in resolving actual cases involving peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate the concrete doctrinal instability that results from the unresolved theoretical tension between consent-based validity and peremptory override.

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide a counterexample to the claim that jus cogens norms have any practical effect in domestic legal systems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that torture should be recognized as a jus cogens norm by all domestic courts, regardless of their national legal traditions.

explanations.correct: The reference appears immediately after the author states that the theoretical tension between consent and peremptory override 'generates concrete doctrinal instability.' The immunity example is introduced as an illustration of that instability — specifically, the problem of determining whether two norms operate at the same hierarchical tier. C captures this rhetorical function.
explanations.A: Sovereign immunity is not addressed again in the remainder of the passage; it is a brief illustrative reference, not an introduction to a new topic.
explanations.B: The passage does not say which theoretical account is more successful in actual cases; it says the tension 'has never been satisfactorily resolved.'
explanations.D: The reference does not serve as a counterexample to jus cogens' practical effect; it illustrates the difficulty of applying it, not its ineffectiveness.
explanations.E: The passage makes no such prescriptive argument about domestic courts and torture; this overstates and misdirects the reference's purpose.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the critics' objection — described in the third paragraph — that the tribunal's reliance on lex specialis effectively circumvents the hierarchy established by the Vienna Convention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The regional treaty frameworks at issue were drafted with explicit provisions acknowledging that obligations under the Vienna Convention's jus cogens articles would remain operative and could not be displaced by the regional regime.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several of the states party to the regional treaty frameworks had also ratified the Vienna Convention and were subject to both instruments simultaneously.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The International Law Commission's list of recognized peremptory norms was not expanded during the period covered by the tribunal's provisional measures orders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The procedural rulings issued under the lex specialis regime had no bearing on whether the underlying substantive conduct at issue violated the prohibition on genocide.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tribunals operating under different regional frameworks had reached the opposite conclusion and applied jus cogens norms over lex specialis objections during the same period.

explanations.correct: The critics' objection is that using lex specialis in procedural contexts 'effectively circumvents' jus cogens — that is, procedural formalism insulates state conduct from scrutiny under peremptory norms. If the procedural rulings had no bearing on the underlying substantive jus cogens question (genocide), then no circumvention actually occurred: the hierarchy was not compromised because the substantive peremptory norm remained fully available for scrutiny on the merits. This directly undermines the critics' claim.
explanations.A: This would strengthen the critics' objection, not undermine it: if the regional regime expressly preserved jus cogens obligations yet the tribunal still applied lex specialis to displace scrutiny, the circumvention would be more, not less, egregious.
explanations.B: Dual ratification is consistent with the critics' complaint; it does not address whether the lex specialis ruling actually insulated conduct from jus cogens scrutiny.
explanations.C: The ILC's enumeration activity is irrelevant to whether the tribunal's procedural approach circumvented the Convention's hierarchy; this is an off-target claim.
explanations.E: Contrary practice by other tribunals would weaken the precedential force of the orders described but would not address whether those specific orders actually circumvented jus cogens — it is an outside-scope claim that bears on consistency, not on the logical force of the critics' circumvention argument.
